inputs.need:
I am a consultant radiologist and lead for imaging stewardship in a health region with four hospitals and about 90 primary care practices. Lumbar spine MRI requests have grown every year, and when we sampled 300 requests for low back pain last spring, 34 percent had no red flag, no radiculopathy and no documented trial of conservative care. The region is about to buy an electronic decision support tool that checks imaging orders against appropriateness criteria at the moment of ordering, and the procurement board wants to know what such tools actually achieve before it writes the specification.

We would like to do an umbrella review: there are already many reviews of imaging decision support, some specific to low back pain, and I would rather bring them together properly than add another pooled analysis of the same trials. The questions are whether decision support reduces inappropriate imaging, whether it changes imaging volume, whether patients are any worse off, how often clinicians override the advice, and whether effects differ for people in deprived areas or with limited English.

I need help with the question, how to find and judge the reviews, what to do when several reviews include the same primary studies, how to handle reviews that disagree, and how to present the findings to a procurement board that is not clinical. A colleague keeps citing one famous multicentre study with a 40 percent effect that I have never been able to find.
inputs.constraints: Review must be finished by 2027-03-31 for the procurement board. One information specialist for 10 days and two reviewers part time. English-language reviews only unless a translator can be found.

records.title: Clinical decision support for diagnostic imaging orders: a systematic review of effects on appropriateness and volume
records.authors: Okafor-Lindahl P, Brandt-Nakamura S, Idowu-Fischer R
records.venue: Journal of Imaging Quality and Safety
records.abstract: We included 32 studies of electronic clinical decision support at the point of ordering diagnostic imaging, 6 of them randomised. Across 14 studies that reported appropriateness, the proportion of inappropriate orders fell by a pooled relative 27 percent (95 percent CI 18 to 35 percent). Effects on imaging volume were smaller and inconsistent. Studies in which clinicians could ignore the advice without giving a reason showed smaller effects. Few studies reported patient outcomes, and most were uncontrolled before-after comparisons from academic centres. We rated the certainty of the evidence as low.

records.title: Decision support for lumbar spine imaging in adults with low back pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Ferreira-Holm K, Achebe-Tanaka L, Morrow-Singh V
records.abstract: We included 11 studies of decision support for lumbar spine imaging in adults presenting with low back pain in primary care or emergency departments. Decision support reduced lumbar imaging orders for non-specific low back pain (risk ratio 0.78, 95 percent CI 0.66 to 0.92). Of the included studies, 2 randomised trials measured pain and function at 3 months and found no differences between groups. Heterogeneity was substantial, largely explained by whether the tool required a reason to override. No study reported outcomes by socioeconomic group or language.

records.title: Interventions to reduce low-value imaging for low back pain: an overview of reviews
records.abstract: We identified 9 reviews of interventions to reduce imaging for low back pain. Audit and feedback, decision support at ordering and targeted education were the interventions with the most consistent reductions in imaging. Confidence in the reviews was low: 4 of the 9 reviews were rated critically low on a standard appraisal tool, mainly because they did not assess risk of bias in included studies. The overview did not account for primary studies included in more than one review and did not report patient outcomes.

records.title: Override of imaging decision support advice by clinicians: a systematic review
records.abstract: We reviewed 19 studies that reported how often clinicians overrode imaging decision support advice. Override rates ranged from 49 to 96 percent of alerts that advised against an order. Overrides were more frequent when alerts fired for orders already judged urgent, when the tool gave no alternative, and in emergency departments. Tools that required a structured reason to override had lower override rates. Few studies examined whether overridden orders were later judged appropriate, and none measured effects on patients whose orders were cancelled after an alert.

records.title: Imaging for low back pain in adults: clinical practice guideline
records.authors: Low Back Pain Guideline Development Group
records.abstract: The guideline recommends against routine imaging for adults with low back pain without red flags, and against imaging within the first six weeks for non-specific pain. Imaging is recommended for suspected cauda equina syndrome, malignancy, infection or fracture, and for radiculopathy persisting after six weeks when surgery or injection is being considered. The guideline notes that imaging without an indication is associated with more further investigation and treatment without better outcomes. Evidence was graded low to moderate for most recommendations.

records.title: Methodological quality and overlap of systematic reviews of imaging decision support: an appraisal with AMSTAR 2
records.abstract: We appraised 26 systematic reviews of decision support for imaging orders with AMSTAR 2. Confidence was rated critically low for 15 reviews and low for 7, most often because protocols were not registered and excluded studies were not listed. The primary studies overlapped substantially across reviews, with a corrected covered area of 18 percent, so counting reviews would double-count the same evidence. Reviews that reported larger effects more often included uncontrolled studies. The authors recommend overlap matrices and AMSTAR 2 ratings in any overview.

records.title: Do imaging stewardship interventions affect groups differently? A scoping review of equity reporting
records.authors: Mahlangu-Reid C, Soto-Brennan P, Fitzgerald-Ude N
records.abstract: We mapped 38 studies of interventions to reduce low-value imaging and recorded whether they reported effects by socioeconomic position, ethnicity, language, age or sex. Only 4 of 38 studies reported any subgroup effect, and none reported effects by language. Two studies found that reductions in imaging were smaller among patients from deprived areas, while one found no difference. Most studies were from academic centres in high-income settings. The review concludes that the equity effects of imaging stewardship are largely unknown and recommends routine subgroup reporting.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Reviews report that decision support reduces inappropriate imaging orders and lumbar imaging for low back pain, with no signal of harm in the few trials that measured pain and function, but most underlying studies are uncontrolled and many reviews are of critically low quality with heavily overlapping primary studies. Clinicians override most alerts unless a reason is required. Equity effects are largely unreported. The multicentre study with a 40 percent effect suggested by the discovery call is a model lead that no retrieved record contains.

response.reading: The procurement question sits on a crowded, overlapping and often low-quality review literature. Effects on appropriateness and orders are consistent in direction but come from uncontrolled studies that reviews count repeatedly. Override behaviour and alert design decide whether a tool works in practice, and equity effects are almost unreported. The famous 40 percent figure is an unverified lead.
